proxy_statement: THIS IS AN OBJECTIVE PROXY, NOT A HUMAN STUDY. No human subjects were recruited, tested, surveyed or observed for this metric and no human-comprehension result is claimed, implied or extrapolated. The proxy consists of two first-party-artifact indicators (R1 canonical machine-enforced form, R2 official style guide) and three scored text-geometry measurements over the frozen benchmark source corpus (R3 line length, R4 nesting depth, R6 routine length), plus R5 sigil density which is measured and published but not scored. It measures surface regularity and surface complexity, not comprehension, learnability or subjective clarity.

cross_language_consistency_note: Level meaning was held constant by five mechanisms. (1) ONE SCRIPT, ONE HASH: readability_proxy.py was SHA-256 verified against the frozen value before any language was measured and then run unchanged, with identical flags, for all ten; every per-language lexing fact came from the document's frozen_lexing_table, not from the scorer. (2) ONE CORPUS SHAPE: the same 11 micro workloads, hand-written implementation sources only, 11 files per language; the same 3 workloads (SVM, GMM, LightGrad) are missing for all ten, so no language was measured over a set another was not. (3) ONE FORMATTER PROTOCOL: for every language the formatter was run twice over an identical scratch copy of the corpus with its documented default invocation and no style flags, and idempotency was decided by `diff -r` between the two passes - a byte-identical result was required, never inferred. Every language was checked for a formatter on this host by the same three probes (PATH lookup, toolchain bin listing, toolchain --help grep). (4) ONE DOCUMENT TEST for R2: a written style and/or naming-convention guide, published by a member of that language's frozen official_project_set, retrieved live over the network with the HTTP status and a verbatim excerpt recorded. That test admitted project-internal conventions documents uniformly - the LLVM Coding Standards for C++, the Microsoft Coding guidelines for TypeScript and the quidra-lang LLM guide for Quidra all describe conventions for that project's own code and were all admitted; admitting one and refusing another would have been the inconsistency. (5) POST-HOC EQUIVALENCE CHECK: the ten assignments were re-read together. The three languages at 60 (Python, TypeScript, Quidra) each fail exactly two scored indicators; the six languages at 80 (C++, Go, Java, Kotlin, Swift, Zig) each fail exactly one; Rust alone fails none. No two languages with the same satisfied-indicator set received different levels, and no two with different sets received the same level by any route other than the frozen count. Ties were left as ties: global_rules.tie_handling forbids breaking them.
fairness_notes: No age adjustment, young-language allowance, potential-based credit or incumbency discount was applied. Quidra 0.2.0 was measured with the same script, the same corpus shape and the same formatter and documentation tests as the other nine.

Quidra's R1 is SATISFIED on its merits and this is reported unchanged: `quidra fmt` exists in the 0.2.0 toolchain, ran over all 11 corpus files with exit 0 twice, produced byte-identical output on the second run, and demonstrably restores canonical spacing (a deliberately de-spaced copy of mb02.qui was restored byte-identically to the committed source). Four established languages - Python, Java, TypeScript and Kotlin - do not satisfy R1 here. That is the measured result, not an adjustment.
Conversely, Quidra's R4 and R6 failures are reported unchanged and are what holds it to 60 alongside Python and TypeScript.

Evidence was collected in the frozen global_rules.evidence_collection_order (Python, C++, Rust, Go, Java, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, Zig, Quidra). Quidra was measured LAST; no threshold, admissibility reading or procedure was settled after seeing Quidra's result.
proxy_limitations_published_with_the_sco: The corpus measurements are taken over code authored for this benchmark and reflect both the language and the authoring of the implementations.
Text geometry is not comprehension. A language may score low on this proxy and still be easy for a human to read, and the reverse.
Thresholds are absolute, were fixed before any measurement, and were not calibrated against any language's measured value.

R1 AND R3 ARE CORRELATED BY CONSTRUCTION: languages satisfying R1 are measured on canonical-formatter output, and canonical formatters typically enforce a line-length limit, which is what R3 measures. Every one of the ten satisfied R3 regardless, so the correlation did not separate any language this run.

The measurement basis differs between languages for that same reason - formatter output for C++, Rust, Go, Swift, Zig and Quidra; committed sources for Python, Java, TypeScript and Kotlin. Small differences in R3 are therefore not pure language properties.

THE TWO BLOCK MODELS ARE NOT ON EXACTLY THE SAME SCALE FOR R4. The indentation model reads approximately one level deeper than the braces model for the same control-flow structure, which makes R4 marginally HARDER for the two indentation-model languages, Quidra and Python. Both are the only two languages that failed R4, and both failed it on p95 alone (6 against a threshold of 5) while satisfying the median conjunct. A reader must not compare R4 numbers across block models without this offset. It is a measurement artefact, not a language property, and the frozen document directs that it be disclosed rather than corrected.

R5 (sigil density) is measured and published but NOT scored. All ten languages fell below the 0.30 threshold (range 0.159 Quidra to 0.272 Go), confirming the pre-freeze expectation that the indicator carries no discriminating information.
limitations: CORPUS INCOMPLETE FOR ALL TEN LANGUAGES: the SVM, GMM and LightGrad implementations (spec 13-15) do not exist in any of the ten languages, so R3, R4 and R6 were measured over the 11 micro workloads only, roughly 685-963 code lines and 32-49 routines per language. The gap is identical across languages, but a fuller corpus could move the p95 statistics, which is where five of the ten languages fail R6 and two fail R4.

R1 UNVERIFIABLE FOR PYTHON AND KOTLIN RATHER THAN ABSENT: a formatter that is plausibly admissible exists for each (black, published in the PSF GitHub organisation; the JetBrains IntelliJ IDEA formatter) but neither is installed on this host and global_rules.host_verification.no_installation_of_extra_software forbids installing it. Both are recorded NOT SATISFIED with verification_status=unverified and availability_state=S3, per global_rules.indicator_model.unverifiable_rule, which the document applies identically to all ten including Quidra. Had black been installed and been ruled first-party, Python would score 80 instead of 60. This is a host-provisioning artefact and belongs in host_limited_indicators.json.

QUIDRA'S TOOLCHAIN WAS BUILT FROM SOURCE ON THIS HOST by the benchmark team, so no Quidra indicator can fail for a repackaging reason, while Python's and Kotlin's R1 did. This asymmetry is disclosed, not corrected.

TYPESCRIPT R2 RESTS ON A RECORDED SCORING DECISION. Microsoft publishes 'Coding guidelines' in the microsoft/TypeScript repository wiki, which is not literally inside TypeScript's frozen official_docs_root; the three URLs that are (typescriptlang.org/docs, nodejs.org/docs, docs.npmjs.com) were examined and contain no style or naming-convention guide. It was admitted for symmetry with Quidra's own frozen, repository-inclusive docs root. Under the narrow reading TypeScript scores 40, not 60. No other language's level changes under either reading.

R2 WAS SCORED ON EXISTENCE, NOT ON SCOPE OR QUALITY. The rubric asks only whether a first-party written style/naming guide exists. The admitted artifacts differ greatly in ambition - PEP 8, the Rust Style Guide and the Kotlin coding conventions are user-facing style guides, while the LLVM Coding Standards, the Microsoft Coding guidelines and Quidra's llm-guide.md are conventions for that project's own or generated code. The indicator does not distinguish them and neither did this scoring.

JAVA'S R2 CHAIN PASSES THROUGH A 1999 DOCUMENT. The OpenJDK Developers' Guide 'Code Conventions' section links Oracle's 'Code Conventions for the Java Programming Language', retrieved at HTTP 200 and marked 'Revised April 20, 1999'. R2 has no recency window, so this satisfies the indicator as written; a reader should know the age.
NO HUMAN-COMPREHENSION CLAIM IS MADE OR IMPLIED anywhere in this record. No human study was performed and none may be inferred from these numbers.
